title: Rectangle Area
description: Brute force to optimized: discretizing the plane into unit cells versus direct inclusion-exclusion using both areas and the overlap rectangle.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given the coordinates of two axis-aligned rectangles, each described by its bottom-left and top-right corners, return the total area covered by the two rectangles combined (counting any overlapping region only once).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: Given two rectangles that may or may not overlap, find the total area of the region covered by at least one of them.

blocks.title: Analogy: Combining the Area of Two Overlapping Tarps
blocks.text: Picture laying two rectangular tarps on the ground, possibly overlapping. The total ground covered is not simply the sum of both tarps' areas, since that would double-count wherever they overlap; the overlapping patch must be subtracted out once.

blocks.caption: Adding both areas double-counts the overlap; subtract it once to correct for that

blocks.text: These two rectangles overlap in a small region; the total covered area is 45.
Both rectangles are identical, fully overlapping each other, so the total covered area is just the area of one of them, 16.
Before trying to reason about the combined shape directly, notice that inclusion-exclusion handles the double-counting problem cleanly: add both areas, then subtract whatever they share.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the two rectangles do not overlap at all, the total area is simply the sum of their two areas.

Observation 2: If they do overlap, that shared region gets counted once in area1 and once again in area2, so it has been counted one time too many.

Observation 3: The overlap of two axis-aligned rectangles is itself always an axis-aligned rectangle (or nothing, if they don't truly overlap), whose width is the overlap of their x-ranges and whose height is the overlap of their y-ranges.

Observation 4: Computing that overlap width and height directly, clamping to 0 when there is no actual overlap, gives the exact correction needed.

This leads directly to inclusion-exclusion: compute both rectangles' areas, compute their overlap rectangle's area (0 if they don't truly overlap), and return the sum of the two areas minus the overlap.
Discretize the plane into a fine grid of unit cells, mark every cell covered by either rectangle, and count the marked cells.

items: Determine the overall bounding region covering both rectangles.
For every unit cell within that region, check whether it falls inside rectangle A or rectangle B.
Count every cell that falls inside at least one of them.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: discretize into unit cells, mark and count cells covered by either rectangle

codes.python:
def compute_area(ax1, ay1, ax2, ay2, bx1, by1, bx2, by2):
    min_x = min(ax1, bx1)
    max_x = max(ax2, bx2)
    min_y = min(ay1, by1)
    max_y = max(ay2, by2)
    count = 0
    for x in range(min_x, max_x):                  # scan every unit cell in the bounding region
        for y in range(min_y, max_y):
            in_a = ax1 <= x < ax2 and ay1 <= y < ay2
            in_b = bx1 <= x < bx2 and by1 <= y < by2
            if in_a or in_b:
                count += 1
    return count

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every unit cell in the entire bounding region is checked individually against both rectangles.
This correctly counts the covered area, but scales with the full coordinate range, not just the rectangles' actual sizes.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(width times height) of the bounding region, potentially enormous given coordinates up to 10000.
Space: O(1) beyond the running count.
Limitation: discretizing into unit cells scales with the coordinate range, not the problem's true complexity, direct geometric formulas make this entirely unnecessary.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why discretizing is unnecessary: rectangle areas, and the overlap of two axis-aligned rectangles, all have simple closed-form formulas, no need to inspect individual points.

How to compute the overlap directly: the overlapping region's x-range is [max of the two left edges, min of the two right edges], and similarly for the y-range; if either range is empty (max exceeds min), there is no overlap.

The core idea: compute both rectangles' areas directly, compute the overlap rectangle's area directly (clamped to 0 if no true overlap), and apply inclusion-exclusion: total equals area1 plus area2 minus the overlap.

Compute area1 and area2 directly from their corner coordinates. Compute the overlap width as the overlap of the two x-ranges, and the overlap height as the overlap of the two y-ranges, each clamped to at least 0. Multiply for the overlap area, and return area1 plus area2 minus that overlap.
Dry run for rectangle A = (-3,0,3,4), rectangle B = (0,-1,9,2)

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: compute both areas and the overlap directly, apply inclusion-exclusion

codes.python:
def compute_area(ax1, ay1, ax2, ay2, bx1, by1, bx2, by2):
    area1 = (ax2 - ax1) * (ay2 - ay1)
    area2 = (bx2 - bx1) * (by2 - by1)
    overlap_x = max(0, min(ax2, bx2) - max(ax1, bx1))    # 0 if the x-ranges don't truly overlap
    overlap_y = max(0, min(ay2, by2) - max(ay1, by1))    # 0 if the y-ranges don't truly overlap
    return area1 + area2 - overlap_x * overlap_y            # inclusion-exclusion

blocks.text: Any point covered by both rectangles is counted once in area1 and once in area2, so it has been counted exactly one extra time; subtracting the overlap area corrects for exactly that double-count, and no more. The overlap rectangle's dimensions follow directly from intersecting the two x-ranges and the two y-ranges, clamped to 0 whenever the rectangles do not truly overlap in that dimension.

blocks.text: Rectangle Area is a straightforward application of inclusion-exclusion: add both areas, then subtract the overlap once, where the overlap itself is computed directly from intersecting the two rectangles' x and y ranges.

items: Forgetting to clamp the overlap width or height to 0 when the rectangles do not actually overlap in that dimension, which would otherwise produce a negative "overlap" that corrupts the result.
Computing the overlap using the wrong combination of min/max (using max of the right edges instead of min, or similar mix-ups).

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do you avoid double-counting the overlap", think: inclusion-exclusion, subtract the overlap area once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(coordinate range squared) time; the optimized inclusion-exclusion formula runs in O(1) time. Both use O(1) space.

items: Pattern: inclusion-exclusion applied to two overlapping rectangles.
Core Idea: total area equals both rectangles' areas added together minus their overlap; the overlap's dimensions come directly from intersecting the two x-ranges and two y-ranges.
Time: O(coordinate range squared) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: the overlap of two axis-aligned rectangles is itself an axis-aligned rectangle, directly computable, or empty.
Interview Difficulty: a straightforward geometry problem once inclusion-exclusion is recognized.
One line memory trick: add both areas, subtract the overlap once.
